lead: Counting rules answer “how many?” without listing every object. The sum rule adds the sizes of disjoint cases. The product rule multiplies the number of options at independent stages. These two rules are the base of most combinatorics: booking forms, menu combos, passwords and test-case counts. The numbers stay small here; the real work is checking that cases do not overlap and that stages do not affect each other.
prereq: You need: set operations for disjoint unions (see Unit 2, Sets, Relations and Functions) and basic proof language (see Unit 1, Logic and Proof Techniques).

blocks.text: Let A be a finite set. Write |A| for the number of elements in A. Suppose A is split into k cases A₁, A₂, …, Aₖ. The cases are disjoint when no object lies in two cases. They are exhaustive when every object lies in at least one case. If both hold, the sum rule says:

blocks.where: A₁, …, Aₖ are pairwise disjoint finite sets that together form A; k is the number of cases.

blocks.text: Example. A metro card can be topped up by 4 UPI apps, 3 bank pages or 2 counter windows. These are three disjoint cases, so the number of methods is 4 + 3 + 2 = 9. If one UPI app also appears on a bank page, the cases overlap; adding would count that app twice.
A decision tree shows the rule: draw one branch for each case, then add the branch sizes. Some syllabi call this the addition principle; the condition, not the name, is what matters.
A choice has k stages. Stage i has nᵢ options. The stages are independent when every choice made earlier still allows all nᵢ options at stage i. Then the number of ordered outcomes is:

blocks.where: N is the number of ordered stage-by-stage outcomes; nᵢ is the number of options at stage i; k is the number of stages.

blocks.text: Example. A thali has 3 rice options, 4 curries and 2 sweets. A meal is one rice, one curry and one sweet, so the count is 3 × 4 × 2 = 24. If the curries depend on the rice chosen, the stages are not independent and this product is wrong.

The table reads a booking form: 4 classes, 3 quotas and 5 payment methods give 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 custom orders. The running product is the partial count after each stage. Some syllabi call this the multiplication principle.
Many counts need both rules. Split the whole set into disjoint cases. Inside each case, multiply independent stages. Then add the case totals. The order is: case first, stage second.

The railway form in the worked example has two cases. Case 1: build a ticket from one class, one quota and one payment method. The product is 4 × 3 × 5 = 60. Case 2: pick one of 6 preset tatkal combos. The preset is one choice, so its size is 6. The cases are disjoint: a custom ticket is not a preset combo. Sum rule gives 60 + 6 = 66.

For a simple combinatorial proof, let S be the set of outcomes. Partition S into S₁, …, Sₖ. A partition means each outcome is in exactly one part. Count each part. The sum rule says |S| is the sum of the part sizes. For the product rule, the outcomes are k-tuples (x₁, …, xₖ), where xᵢ comes from a set of size nᵢ; the number of such tuples is the product.

Two checks catch most errors. Disjointness: can one outcome appear in two cases? Independence: after an early choice, does every later option remain available, with the same count? If either check fails, repair the cases or use inclusion–exclusion (see 3.4). Ordered stages count sequences; if order does not matter, do not use the product rule blindly (see 3.2).

examples.question: An IRCTC booking form offers 4 travel classes, 3 quotas and 5 payment methods. A passenger either builds a ticket from one class, one quota and one payment method, or picks one of 6 preset tatkal combos. How many ticket-building choices are there?
steps: Split the choices into two disjoint cases: a custom ticket and a preset tatkal combo.
Custom ticket: 3 independent stages, with 4 class options, 3 quota options and 5 payment options.
Product rule for the custom case: 4 × 3 × 5 = 60.
Preset case: 6 single choices. This case is disjoint from the custom case because a preset combo is not built from separate class, quota and payment choices.
Sum rule for the two cases: 60 + 6 = 66.

print(custom)

traps: Adding overlapping cases. If one outcome can appear in two cases, the sum rule overcounts; use inclusion–exclusion (3.4) or redefine the cases.
Multiplying dependent stages. If a choice at stage 2 changes the number of options at stage 3, n₁×n₂×n₃ is not valid.
Using the product rule for unordered selections. Product counts sequences; choosing a captain then a vice-captain gives 11×10 ordered pairs, not 2-player teams (see 3.2).
Forgetting the single-choice case. A preset combo is one option, not a stage with several parts; do not multiply it by class or quota.
Not checking exhaustiveness. Cases must cover all outcomes; a missing case gives a total that is too small.

quiz.q: State the product rule for k independent stages.
quiz.a: If stage i has nᵢ options and the stages are independent, total ordered outcomes = n₁ × n₂ × ⋯ × nₖ.

quiz.q: Why does the sum rule require disjoint cases?
quiz.a: An outcome in two cases would be counted twice; adding sizes is valid only when every outcome belongs to exactly one case.

quiz.q: A cafe has 3 breads, 4 fillings and 2 drinks. A meal is one of each. A combo list has 5 preset meals. How many choices?
A code is 2 letters (26 choices each) followed by 3 digits (10 choices each), repetition allowed. Count the codes.
A survey says 40 take tea, 35 take coffee, so 75 take tea or coffee. What is missing? If 10 take both, give the correct count.
quiz.a: The sets may overlap. The sum rule needs disjoint cases. Correct count = 40 + 35 − 10 = 65.

quiz.q: A form offers 5 plans or 2 add-ons. A student may pick a plan and any add-on. Is 5 + 2 correct? Give the count if every add-on works with every plan.
quiz.a: No; these are stages, not disjoint cases. Product = 5 × 2 = 10 plan-add-on pairs. The sum 7 counts single items only.

quiz.q: In a tree diagram, which branches are multiplied and which are added?
quiz.a: Branches at successive stages of one case are multiplied; separate alternative cases are added after each case is counted.

beyond: Not for the exam. These rules are the arithmetic behind password-strength meters, combinatorial test design and state-space estimates in algorithms. A search for “rule of product combinatorics” and “combinatorial testing pairwise” leads to industry material. Generating functions, later in this unit, turn product and sum rules into algebra on series.
